claim: The core of the auditory processing system in songbirds consists of anatomical areas named Field L, NCM (caudomedial nidopallium), and CM (caudomedial mesopalium).
source: The core of the auditory processing system consists of anatomical areas named Field L, NCM (caudomedial nidopallium), and CM (caudomedial mesopalium) (Vates et al., 1996) (Figure 1c).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vates et al., 1996 and reference to Figure 1c

claim: Field L is composed of four different sub-regions: L2a, L2b, L1, and L3 that are reciprocally connected.
source: Field L, the primary thalamorecipient area, is composed of four different sub-regions (L2a, L2b, L1, and L3) that are reciprocally connected (Vates et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vates et al., 1996

claim: L2a receives the strongest input from the core of Ov (nucleus ovoidalis), the primary auditory thalamus.
source: Among these sub-regions, L2a receives the strongest input from the core of Ov (nucleus ovoidalis), the primary auditory thalamus (Müller and Leppelsack, 1985; Rübsamen and Dörrscheidt, 1986; Hose et al., 1987).
evidence: Supported by citations to Müller and Leppelsack, 1985; Rübsamen and Dörrscheidt, 1986; Hose et al., 1987

claim: Secondary auditory areas L2b, L3, and L1 receive feed-forward input from L2a and thalamus, but also receive feedback from higher cortical areas such as CM.
source: Secondary auditory areas — L2b, L3, and L1 — receive feed-forward input from L2a and thalamus, but also receive feedback from higher cortical areas such as CM.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript text

claim: Temporal cues in song provide reliable information about the identity of the singer in zebra finches and other songbirds.
source: For zebra finches and other songbirds, temporal cues in song provide reliable information about the identity of the singer and are used for perceptual discrimination of songs (Gentner and Margoliash, 2003; Gentner et al., 2006; Grace et al., 2003; Shaevitz and Theunissen, 2007).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to Gentner and Margoliash, 2003; Gentner et al., 2006; Grace et al., 2003; Shaevitz and Theunissen, 2007

claim: Neurons from midbrain to the highest levels of auditory association areas in zebra finches respond with precise spike times to playback of conspecific song.
source: In the zebra finch auditory system, there are neurons from midbrain to the highest levels of auditory association areas that respond with precise spike times to playback of conspecific song.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript text

claim: Sparse-firing neurons in NCM respond with precise spike times to playback of conspecific song.
source: This is true for both dense-spiking neurons and the highly selective, sparse-firing neurons recently described in the high-level auditory area, NCM (Schneider and Woolley, 2013), as well as in the auditory-motor association area, HVC (high vocal center) (Prather et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schneider and Woolley, 2013

claim: The effective temporal integration window of neurons in L2a is very brief compared with responses in areas L1 and L3.
source: Using a spectrotemporal receptive field (STRF) analysis, the effective temporal integration window of neurons in L2a, the first thalamorecipient zone, was observed to be very brief compared with responses one step further from the periphery in areas L1 and L3 (Kim and Doupe, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kim and Doupe, 2011

claim: Secondary areas L2b, L1, and L3 receive significant feedback from high-order auditory areas, but the primary zone L2a does not.
source: The secondary areas (including L2b, L1, and L3) but not the primary zone (L2a) are recipients of significant feedback from high-order auditory areas (Vates et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vates et al., 1996

claim: Neurons responding to song in secondary areas L2b and L3 become less synchronous in their relative response times compared to those in the primary area L2a.
source: We first demonstrate that neurons responding to song in secondary areas, L2b and L3, become less synchronous in their relative response times yet more informative about the identity of specific syllables when compared to those in the primary area, L2a.
evidence: Supported by data presented in the manuscript

claim: Neurons responding to song in secondary areas L2b and L3 are more informative about the identity of specific syllables compared to those in the primary area L2a.
source: We first demonstrate that neurons responding to song in secondary areas, L2b and L3, become less synchronous in their relative response times yet more informative about the identity of specific syllables when compared to those in the primary area, L2a.
evidence: Supported by data presented in the manuscript, including Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: In the primary zone L2a, each click elicits a similar low-latency response in all recorded neurons, largely insensitive to the temporal context of the click.
source: In the primary zone, each click elicited a similar low-latency response in all recorded neurons, and the structure of this response was largely insensitive to the temporal context of the click.
evidence: Supported by data presented in the manuscript, including Figure 3

claim: In secondary auditory areas L2b and L3, neurons respond asynchronously and selectively, depending on the temporal context of the click.
source: One synapse further from the periphery, in secondary auditory areas, L2b and L3, neurons responded asynchronously and selectively, depending on the temporal context of the click.
evidence: Supported by data presented in the manuscript, including Figure 3

claim: Temporal sequences are transformed to distinct population vectors in the transition from primary to secondary auditory areas.
source: In effect, temporal sequences are transformed to distinct population vectors in the transition from primary to secondary auditory areas.
evidence: Supported by data presented in the manuscript, including Figure 4

claim: Zebra finches rapidly learned to discriminate click sequences composed of song-like intervals using a 'restart-go' operant paradigm.
source: Using this training procedure, zebra finches rapidly learned to discriminate click sequences that were composed of song-like intervals.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data presented in the manuscript, including Figure 6

claim: When the stimulus set was slowed by a factor of two, the strength of the temporal to spatial transformation in the secondary auditory area was reduced.
source: When the stimulus set was slowed by a factor of two, the strength of the temporal to spatial transformation in the secondary auditory was reduced, and there was a corresponding degradation of behavioral discrimination.
evidence: Supported by data presented in the manuscript, including Figure 5

claim: When the stimulus set was slowed by a factor of two, there was a corresponding degradation of behavioral discrimination.
source: When the stimulus set was slowed by a factor of two, the strength of the temporal to spatial transformation in the secondary auditory was reduced, and there was a corresponding degradation of behavioral discrimination.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data presented in the manuscript, including Figure 6c

claim: The ascending auditory pathway in zebra finches transforms temporal sequences into distinct population vectors.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that the ascending auditory pathway in zebra finches transforms temporal sequences into distinct population vectors.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from data presented in the manuscript

claim: The transformation of temporal sequences to distinct population vectors applies to click sequences consisting of intervals that overlap with sub-syllabic acoustic structure in song.
source: This transformation applied to click sequences consisting of intervals that overlap with sub-syllabic acoustic structure in song, and may provide an important substrate for song perception and discrimination in sub-syllabic time-scales.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from data presented in the manuscript

claim: The transformation of temporal sequences to distinct population vectors may provide an important substrate for song perception and discrimination in sub-syllabic time-scales.
source: This transformation applied to click sequences consisting of intervals that overlap with sub-syllabic acoustic structure in song, and may provide an important substrate for song perception and discrimination in sub-syllabic time-scales.
evidence: Speculative statement based on data presented in the manuscript

claim: Electrophysiological recordings were gathered using four-shank, 32 channel silicon electrodes.
source: General note: the electrophysiological recordings reported here were gathered using four-shank, 32 channel silicon electrodes.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript text

claim: Activity was recorded simultaneously from the primary thalamorecipient zone in the auditory area, Field L2a, and neighboring auditory areas in L2b and L3.
source: From each bird, we recorded activity simultaneously from the primary thalamorecipient zone in the auditory area, Field L2a, and neighboring auditory areas in L2b and L3 (Figure 1a and b).
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 1

claim: All stimuli were presented in an interleaved fashion.
source: All stimuli were presented in an interleaved fashion, and each animal was recorded acutely, with all data gathered in a single session.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript text

claim: Each animal was recorded acutely, with all data gathered in a single session.
source: All stimuli were presented in an interleaved fashion, and each animal was recorded acutely, with all data gathered in a single session.

claim: Primary and secondary recording sites were distinguished on the basis of distinct response profiles found in the two areas.
source: Primary and secondary recording sites were distinguished on the basis of the distinct response profiles found in the two areas (Figures 1a and 3a).
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript text with reference to Figures 1a and 3a

claim: The classification of recording sites as primary or secondary was confirmed by spatial mapping showing that primary cells were spatially segregated from secondary neurons.
source: This classification was confirmed by spatial mapping of the recording sites (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), showing that the primary cells were spatially segregated from the secondary neurons.

claim: The primary auditory area L2a could not be reliably identified by spatial coordinates alone due to small anatomical and surgical variations and the small scale of the primary zone.
source: Due to small anatomical and surgical variations and the small scale of the primary zone, this area could not be reliably identified by spatial coordinates alone.

claim: Precise spike timing could be found in both primary and secondary areas in response to song.
source: Precise spike timing could be found in both primary and secondary areas in response to song.

evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and Figure 2a

claim: Neurons in secondary auditory areas L2b and L3 showed a broader repertoire of response profiles compared to L2a.
source: By contrast, neurons in secondary auditory areas, L2b and L3, showed a broader repertoire of response profiles.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript text

claim: The increase in the diversity of response timing in secondary auditory areas leads to a decrease in the magnitude of the cross-correlation between the PSTHs of individual neurons relative to primary area L2a.
source: This increase in the diversity of response timing leads to a decrease in the magnitude of the cross-correlation between the PSTHs of individual neurons in the secondary auditory areas relative to a similar cross-correlation performed in primary area, L2a (Figure 1d).
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 1d

claim: The chosen synthetic click stimuli were three seconds long and composed of clicks separated by ten specific inter-click intervals (11, 14, 16, 20, 23, 26, 29, 34, 36 and 40 ms).
source: The chosen synthetic stimuli were three seconds long and composed of clicks separated by ten specific inter-click intervals (11, 14, 16, 20, 23, 26, 29, 34, 36 and 40 ms).
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript text

claim: The inter-click intervals were chosen on the basis of the timescale of neural responses to birdsongs in L2a.
source: We chose these intervals on the basis of the timescale of neural responses to birdsongs in L2a (Figure 2a and b).
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 2a and b

claim: The selected inter-click intervals are similar to intervals between sub-syllabic acoustic transitions found in zebra finch song.
source: We note that the selected inter-click intervals are also similar to intervals between sub-syllabic acoustic transitions found in zebra finch song (Amador et al., 2013; Norton and Scharff, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Amador et al., 2013; Norton and Scharff, 2016

source: The duration of all ten click intervals summed together is 249 ms.

source: The longer three-second sequences were built from 249 ms blocks, in which each block contains a permutation of the ten click intervals.

claim: On timescales longer than the block duration, the statistical properties of all click stimuli were equivalent.
source: On timescales longer than the block duration, the statistical properties of all stimuli were equivalent.

claim: The click sequence contains no significant spectral cues for frequencies above 100 Hz.
source: The click sequence, by definition, contains no significant spectral cues for frequencies above 100 Hz (the shortest interval in the click set was 11 ms, thus below the 100 Hz cutoff).
evidence: Logical inference from the definition of the click sequence

claim: Zebra finch hearing thresholds for pure tones are attenuated by about 20 dB relative to humans at 100 Hz.
source: Zebra finch hearing thresholds for pure tones are attenuated by about 20 dB relative to humans at 100 Hz (Okanoya and Dooling, 1987; Moore, 2007), and the fundamental frequency of conspecific song is typically 500 Hz or higher in zebra finches.
evidence: Supported by citations to Okanoya and Dooling, 1987; Moore, 2007

claim: The fundamental frequency of conspecific song is typically 500 Hz or higher in zebra finches.
source: Zebra finch hearing thresholds for pure tones are attenuated by about 20 dB relative to humans at 100 Hz (Okanoya and Dooling, 1987; Moore, 2007), and the fundamental frequency of conspecific song is typically 500 Hz or higher in zebra finches.

claim: In the primary auditory area, the click responses are fairly insensitive to the local context.
source: In the primary auditory area, the click responses are fairly insensitive to the local context – to first approximation, each click evoked a synchronous, low latency response across channels, whereas secondary auditory areas were characterized by sparser and less synchronous responses that were more sensitive to the sequence context of the click (Figure 3—figure supplements 4 and 5).
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 3—figure supplements 4 and 5

claim: Secondary auditory areas were characterized by sparser and less synchronous responses that were more sensitive to the sequence context of the click.
source: In the primary auditory area, the click responses are fairly insensitive to the local context – to first approximation, each click evoked a synchronous, low latency response across channels, whereas secondary auditory areas were characterized by sparser and less synchronous responses that were more sensitive to the sequence context of the click (Figure 3—figure supplements 4 and 5).
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 3—figure supplements 4 and 5

claim: In the primary auditory area L2a, the phase-space trajectories of distinct stimuli overlap for all time points.
source: In the primary auditory area, L2a, the phase-space trajectories of distinct stimuli overlap for all time points, meaning that the pattern of active cells contains little population-vector information that can distinguish the stimuli.
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 4a

claim: In secondary auditory areas, specific points in the phase-space trajectory diverge from one another in a stimulus-dependent manner.
source: By contrast, in secondary auditory areas, specific points in the phase-space trajectory diverge from one another in a stimulus-dependent manner.
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 4a

claim: The pattern of cell responses in secondary auditory areas contains information about one or more intervals preceding the click.
source: That is, the pattern of cell responses in secondary auditory areas contains information about one or more intervals preceding the click.
evidence: Inference from data presented in the manuscript

claim: ROC analysis reveals enhanced discriminability of click sequences in secondary auditory areas L2b and L3 relative to the primary auditory area L2a.
source: To quantify the degree to which the click stimuli can be distinguished on the basis of the neural responses, we defined a simple decoding mechanism based on the population vector of the ensemble response (see Methods for details). In this decoding, the discriminability of the sequence at a particular time is given by the distance in phase space to the nearest trajectory belonging to a different stimulus. The power of this 'spatial' code for sequence discrimination is quantified through an ROC (receiver operating characteristic) analysis in Figure 4b.
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 4b

claim: The sequence discriminability in secondary auditory areas is maintained even when considering only the first 500 ms of the neural response.
source: We repeated this analysis for just the first 500 ms of the stimulus, and still found a high degree of sequence discriminability in the secondary auditory areas (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: The same ROC analysis applied to song syllable responses found an increase in syllable discriminability in the secondary auditory area.
source: To further validate this approach, we applied the same analysis to the PSTH of the song syllable responses (n = 13 syllables, Figure 1a) and found an increase in syllable discriminability in the secondary auditory area (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: The timescale dilation of click sequences by a factor of two resulted in reduced sequence discrimination in secondary auditory areas.
source: Using the same phase-plane ROC analysis, we found that the timescale dilation led to reduced sequence discrimination in secondary auditory areas (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 5

claim: Slower click sequences evoke a lower spike rate in primary and secondary auditory areas.
source: We next repeated the click electrophysiology using a stimulus set composed of intervals twice as long as those in the first stimulus set (22–80 ms, rather than 11–40 ms, Figure 2c). This change in stimulus timescale had a minimal impact on spike rate in the secondary auditory cortex (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), but resulted in a significant change in the power of the temporal to spatial transformation.
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: Within a population of trained birds (n = 53), a majority (n = 35 birds) showed high levels of performance (d' > 1) within 14 days of training onset.
source: Within a population of trained birds (n = 53), a majority (n = 35 birds) showed high levels of performance (d' > 1) within 14 days of training onset, revealing that songbirds could readily learn to discriminate the fast temporal click sequences used in this study.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data presented in the manuscript

claim: Songbirds could readily learn to discriminate the fast temporal click sequences used in this study.

claim: For time-reversed click stimuli, behavior fell to chance levels.

evidence: Supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 7a

claim: The ordering of the click intervals was critical to the behavioral discrimination.

claim: For cyclic permutations of the training stimuli, a small decrease in performance was found when the cyclic stimulus was first introduced, but within four days, performance returned to baseline.

evidence: Supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 7b

claim: The birds are listening for patterned sequences of intervals irrespective of their absolute time of occurrence relative to the onset of the trial.
source: The conclusion from this is that the birds are listening for patterned sequences of intervals irrespective of their absolute time of occurrence relative to the onset of the trial.

claim: Birds trained to discriminate fast sequences failed to respond above chance levels when the timescale of the clicks was slowed by a factor of two.
source: We found that birds trained to discriminate fast sequences failed to respond above chance levels when the timescale of the clicks was slowed by a factor of two.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data presented in the manuscript

claim: No bird developed a discrimination ability for the slower click sequences when trained exclusively on slower sequences from the outset.
source: We next examined whether naive birds could learn to discriminate the slower click sequences if they were exclusively trained on the slower sequences from the outset. Eleven birds were trained in a single-stage training and four birds were trained on the first stage of a two-stage training procedure that is also documented in the Methods section. In contrast to the high success rate for faster click sequences, no bird developed a discrimination ability for the slower click sequences (Figure 6c, Figure 6—figure supplement 2g and h).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 6c and Figure 6—figure supplement 2g and h

claim: The ability to discriminate click stimuli was found only for the faster click sequences.
source: The ability to discriminate click stimuli was found only for the faster click sequences.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from behavioral data presented in the manuscript
